summary:
Faroe Islands stands under Denmark's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here.

The Faroe Islands are a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark. Domestic equality and family law are set locally, beneath a Danish human-rights framework. Same-sex marriage arrived only in 2017, late for the Nordics, after friction between church and state.

In 2006 LGBT activists gathered around 20,000 online signatures in a population of about 47,000, demanding an end to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and a registered-partnership law aligned with the rest of the Nordics. The territory had neither at that date. Surveys of the period found violence and discrimination against openly gay people not uncommon and legally unaddressed.

Religiously motivated opposition sits openly in Faroese politics. On 7 September 2010 Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for visiting Icelandic prime minister Johanna Sigurdardóttir and her partner, citing his religion. The refusal concerned the presence of an openly gay head of government at an official table.

Opposition to public visibility continued. In July 2015, when av Rana demanded that Pride be banned from its position two days before the national holiday, singer Eivor Pálsdóttir publicly urged people to ignore him. His party remains formally opposed to homosexuality.

For a trans visitor the recorded hostility is political and rhetorical rather than physical. The named targets are openly gay public figures and a Pride event, and the actions on record are a refusal to sit at a banquet and a call for a ban. Violence risk appears low on the sourced material.
tangentialFactors:
The Faroes followed the rest of the Nordics rather than leading them: the 2006 petition was explicitly framed as bringing the territory into line with its neighbours on registered partnership, and equal marriage came only in 2017.

Scale shapes how opposition reads. With a population of roughly 47,000 at the time of the petition, 20,000 signatures represented a very large share of the electorate, and a single MP refusing a banquet draws national attention in a polity of that size.

Pride is scheduled two days before the national holiday, which supplies opponents a framing beyond homosexuality itself. Organised pushback came from a nationally prominent singer rather than from an institution.

The sources bear on sexual orientation. No gender-identity claim appears among them.
localsOnly:
Equality and family law for residents is made in the Faroe Islands, under a Danish human-rights framework; the 2006 signature drive was the instrument used to demand it, at a point when neither anti-discrimination protection nor a registered-partnership law existed locally.

The Centre Party of Jenis av Rana remains formally opposed to homosexuality, and its leader's refusal of a 2010 state banquet was made on religious grounds. Residents have organised counter-mobilisation: Eivor Pálsdóttir's 2015 public call to ignore a Pride ban demand shows domestic cultural pushback from public figures.

Same-sex marriage has been available since 2017, following church-state friction over the change.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no trans-specific source for the Faroe Islands. Gender recognition, identity-document markers, entry screening, facilities, and access to care are unsourced for this jurisdiction and should be treated as unresolved rather than as absent.

Whether Denmark's criminal statutes and document rules apply to the Faroe Islands in full, in part, or with local exceptions is unresolved in the sourced material. The extension asserted above is not itemised by any source here.

The 2006 legal position — no anti-discrimination protection, no registered partnership — is historical. Current Faroese equality and family law beyond the 2017 marriage provision is not sourced.

Population figures differ between sources, about 47,000 in the 2006 account and about 50,000 in later accounts.

The party's formal stance and the MP's positions are sourced only to 2010 and 2015; their current status is not sourced.
